authority.note: Manuscript blessed by Gary 2026-07-29; visual design NOT yet reviewed. Covers three connected places: the yard with its step and gate (beats 1-4), the shed interior (beats 5-16), and the shed roof (beat 17). DRESSING DELIBERATELY DESCRIBES ONE MOMENT ONLY. The shed has a before-the-line and an after-the-line state, but per the lesson recorded on `the-room` (contract.dressing feeds straight into the prompt, and enumerating two states there returned twelve stacked diptychs), the state is carried by each spread's own scene text and NEVER by this contract. 2026-07-29: the `interior-line` plate was RETIRED and the five-machine row deleted from canon, because the story was rewritten away from a pipeline conception. The shed now holds a bench, paper, tools and one throwing arm.

contract.map: THE PLANE SHED: an ordinary small backyard timber shed a child could actually have, roughly three metres by four. Weathered grey-brown VERTICAL BOARD walls and a LOW SINGLE-PITCH ROOF sloping down toward the yard, low enough that a child on an upturned crate can climb onto it. The door is in the SHORT wall facing the yard. ONE SQUARE FOUR-PANE WINDOW sits in the LONG wall, with a WORKBENCH running the full length of that wall beneath it. Shelves and a pegboard above the bench. A single bare bulb on a flex. Outside the door, a LOW CONCRETE STEP of two treads; beyond it a mown grass yard about fifteen metres long ending in a WAIST-HIGH WOODEN GATE, which is the far marker the first plane reaches. NEVER a laboratory, NEVER a factory floor, NEVER a maker-space, NEVER impressive.
contract.blocking: HANDEDNESS IS FIXED AND NEVER CHANGES BETWEEN SPREADS, and this is the single most important rule about this room. In EVERY interior view, without exception: the OPEN DOORWAY is at the LEFT-HAND END of the room with green grass and daylight beyond it; the WORKBENCH runs along the RIGHT-HAND wall, receding away from the doorway; the SQUARE FOUR-PANE WINDOW is in that same right-hand wall, directly ABOVE the bench; the SHELVES and the PEGBOARD are above and beyond the bench on that right-hand wall; the single BARE BULB hangs from the ceiling near the middle. The THROWING ARM, once it exists, is always clamped at the bench end NEAREST THE DOORWAY, which is the LEFT end. There is NO production line and NO row of machines in this shed, ever: the bench holds paper, tools and the single throwing arm. The camera may come closer or pull wider, and may stand anywhere in the room, BUT IT NEVER CROSSES THE ROOM'S AXIS: the doorway is never on the right, the bench and window are never on the left, and the room is never mirrored. It is a SMALL room, three metres by four, and the ceiling is barely above an adult's head. THE BENCH IS BUILT AGAINST THE WALL AND IS NEVER A FREE-STANDING TABLE. It is fixed along the right-hand wall with its back edge touching that wall, directly under the window, and there is NO other table, desk or workbench anywhere in the room. It follows that THE CAMERA IS ALWAYS INSIDE THE ROOM AND NEVER INSIDE OR BEYOND A WALL: you can never see the far side of the bench, and a child working at it is therefore seen FROM BEHIND, from three-quarters behind, or FROM THE SIDE along the bench. A child must NEVER be shown standing behind the bench facing the camera across it, because there is no floor back there to stand on. The bench's near end runs toward the viewer and its far end runs away toward the back of the shed.
contract.dressing: The shed is CLUTTERED, WOODEN and WARM, and everything in it is plainly hand-made by children: loose sheets of paper, a jar of pencils, blunt scissors, string, pencil marks straight on the bench top, folded paper planes lying where they were put down. Light is only daylight through the four-pane window plus one bare bulb; never dramatic, never rim-lit, never moody. RENDER ONE MOMENT IN TIME ONLY: a single view of the shed as it is in this one scene, never a before-and-after, never a split panel, never two versions of the room in one image.
contract.scale: Small enough that two children fill it. A viewer must believe two kids built everything in the room. Pip is a small tin toy no taller than a child's knee and is NEVER as tall as the workbench.

prose.rules: THE SHED MUST NEVER LOOK IMPRESSIVE OR INDUSTRIAL. No soaring space, no banks of equipment, no cables, no monitors, no clean surfaces, no branding. It is small, wooden, cluttered and warm. If a render returns a workshop that reads as a laboratory or a maker-space, regenerate rather than accept.
